odonnell-2020-nature.label: O'Donnell et al., Nature 2020
odonnell-2020-nature.synopsis: We show that tyramine produced by commensal Providencia gut bacteria bypasses host tyramine biosynthesis to manipulate a host sensory decision in C. elegans. Bacterially produced tyramine is converted to octopamine by the host, which then targets OCTR-1 receptors on ASH nociceptive neurons to modulate aversive olfactory behavior. C. elegans colonized by Providencia preferentially select these bacteria in food choice assays, a bias requiring bacterially produced tyramine and host octopamine signaling — demonstrating that a gut bacterium mimics a host neurotransmitter to promote fitness of both partners.

odonnell-2018-plos-genetics.label: O'Donnell et al., PLoS Genetics 2018
odonnell-2018-plos-genetics.synopsis: We show that TORC2 acts in the intestine as a hub for communicating feeding state to the nervous system in C. elegans. During development, intestinal TORC2 regulates neuronal expression of daf-7 TGF-β and daf-28 insulin-like peptide, which reflect bacterial-diet-dependent feeding status and integrate food signals with external cues to control the reproductive growth vs. dauer decision. In adults, intestinal TORC2 similarly modulates food-regulated foraging behavior via PDF-2/PDFR-1 neuropeptide signaling, demonstrating a conserved gut-to-brain axis that adjusts neuronal function according to internal nutritional state.

malaiwong-2025-biorxiv.label: Malaiwong et al., bioRxiv 2025
malaiwong-2025-biorxiv.synopsis: We show that C. elegans synthesizes lipidated neurohormones — conjugates of octopamine and fat metabolism-derived fatty acids — to relay information about lipid metabolic status to the nervous system. The incorporated fatty acids normally act as agonists of NHR-49/PPARα. Intracellular hydrolysis releases free octopamine that activates neuronal receptors to inhibit aversive olfactory responses — but only when prior lipid metabolism has occurred. An intertissue trafficking pathway shuttles octopamine into the intestine for chemical modification before neuronal import, coupling neurotransmitter signaling to lipid homeostasis as a mechanism for state-dependent behavioral regulation.

zang-2026-biorxiv.label: Zang et al., bioRxiv 2026
zang-2026-biorxiv.synopsis: In this collaborative work, we show that the freshwater sponge Spongilla lacustris synthesizes monoamines — tryptamine, phenethylamine, and tyramine — to coordinate canal contraction and relaxation in the absence of neurons or muscles. Tryptamine activates GPCR signaling and Rho GTPases, remodeling adhesion and actomyosin networks in contractile canal epithelia to drive localized constrictions and whole-body deflations. These findings define an ancestral monoaminergic system linking secretory and contractile cell types that predates neurons, suggesting that chemical neurotransmission evolved from pre-neuronal coordination mechanisms later elaborated for synaptic neuromodulation.

bargmann-1991-science.label: Bargmann & Horvitz, Science 1991
bargmann-1991-science.synopsis: Uses laser ablation of identified neurons to map the C. elegans chemosensory system. AWC and AWA neurons detect volatile odorants and mediate olfactory attraction; ASE and ASG detect dissolved ions and drive gustatory responses; ASH responds to noxious chemicals and drives avoidance. Foundational map of chemosensory neuron identities and functions.

bargmann-2006-wormbook.label: Bargmann, WormBook 2006 — Chemosensation
bargmann-2006-wormbook.synopsis: Comprehensive review of C. elegans chemosensation: neuron identities, chemoreceptor gene families, signal transduction via cGMP and calcium channels, and the circuit logic governing approach and avoidance across olfactory and gustatory modalities.

bargmann-1993-cell.label: Bargmann et al., Cell 1993
bargmann-1993-cell.synopsis: Characterizes odorant-selective receptor genes expressed in AWC and AWA neurons; different odorant classes are detected by different neuron subsets, and single neurons can detect and discriminate potentially many odors.

chalfie-1985-j-neurosci.label: Chalfie et al., J Neurosci 1985
chalfie-1985-j-neurosci.synopsis: Defines the mechanosensory touch circuit in C. elegans using electron microscopy circuit reconstruction and laser ablation. Six touch receptor neurons feed into two pathways for anterior touch (via AVD and AVB interneurons) and one pathway for posterior touch (via PVC interneurons). The anterior circuit matures during development: touch cells become coupled by gap junctions and the AVB pathway is added to the pre-existing AVD pathway. Touch cells also synapse broadly onto non-locomotor targets, suggesting touch stimulation modifies multiple behaviors.

white-1986-phil-trans.label: White et al., Phil Trans R Soc B 1986
white-1986-phil-trans.synopsis: The complete electron-microscopic reconstruction of all 302 neurons and approximately 7,000 synaptic connections in C. elegans — the foundational connectome. Remains the structural reference for all circuit-level interpretation in the field, and establishes C. elegans as a model for whole-brain wiring-level analysis.

kaplan-1993-pnas.label: Kaplan & Horvitz, PNAS 1993
kaplan-1993-pnas.synopsis: Characterizes ASH as a polymodal nociceptor that responds to both harsh mechanical stimuli and aversive chemicals — a single neuron integrating multiple threat signals. ASH synapses onto AVA command interneurons to drive rapid reversals, establishing the cellular basis of nociceptive avoidance in C. elegans.

torayama-2007-j-neurosci.label: Torayama et al., J Neurosci 2007
torayama-2007-j-neurosci.synopsis: Demonstrates positive olfactory associative conditioning in C. elegans: pairing the odorant butanone with bacterial food enhances subsequent chemotaxis to butanone. The conditioning requires AWC^ON neuron activity and is modulated by insulin/IGF-1 signaling, revealing a cellular and molecular basis for experience-dependent odor preference.

song-2013-elife.label: Song et al., eLife 2013
song-2013-elife.synopsis: Shows that C. elegans forms a memory of familiar foods and increases its feeding response upon re-encountering them. Recognition of familiar food activates ADF chemosensory neurons, which release serotonin that acts humorally on SER-7 receptors in MC pharyngeal motor neurons to accelerate feeding rate. Novel food overrides this effect by suppressing ADF activity, revealing how familiarity discrimination shapes food intake through a defined chemosensory-to-motor circuit.

zhang-2005-nature.label: Zhang et al., Nature 2005
zhang-2005-nature.synopsis: Landmark paper demonstrating pathogen-conditioned olfactory aversion in C. elegans. Worms that survive exposure to Pseudomonas aeruginosa subsequently avoid the smell of that pathogen. The aversive memory requires serotonin signaling and persists for hours, establishing C. elegans as a model for experience-dependent behavioral immunity.

ha-2010-neuron.label: Ha et al., Neuron 2010
ha-2010-neuron.synopsis: Maps the complete neural circuit for naive and learned olfactory preference in C. elegans from sensory input to motor output. Naive preference for pathogen odors is encoded by AWB and AWC sensory neurons and their downstream interneurons; learned aversion after pathogen exposure requires a separate ADF serotonergic modulatory circuit that alters signal transduction to downstream motor neurons. The behavioral switch between naive and learned preference arises from interplay between these two circuits rather than modification of a single shared pathway.

sawin-2000-neuron.label: Sawin et al., Neuron 2000
sawin-2000-neuron.synopsis: Demonstrates that dopamine and serotonin differentially modulate locomotion based on feeding state: food contact slows locomotion rate via dopamine from CEP/ADE mechanosensory neurons, while recent feeding history promotes pharyngeal pumping and adjusts locomotion via serotonin from NSM neurons. Establishes the monoaminergic basis of food-state-dependent behavior.

hills-2004-j-neurosci.label: Hills et al., J Neurosci 2004
hills-2004-j-neurosci.synopsis: Shows that dopaminergic and glutamatergic signaling co-regulate area-restricted search (ARS) in C. elegans. Dopamine released on food contact modulates glutamatergic signaling via GLR-1/GLR-2 AMPA-type receptors and the EAT-4 vesicular glutamate transporter in the locomotory control circuit, increasing turn frequency to keep worms near food. Loss of either dopamine signaling or glutamate receptor function eliminates ARS; dopamine preincubation restores ARS in dopamine-deficient but not glutamate receptor mutants, placing glutamate downstream of dopamine in the same pathway.

gray-2005-pnas.label: Gray et al., PNAS 2005
gray-2005-pnas.synopsis: Dissects the neural circuit for exploratory behavior in C. elegans. After food removal, AWC olfactory neurons, ASK gustatory neurons, and AIB interneurons drive local search via increased reversals and omega turns; over 30 minutes, ASI gustatory neurons and AIY interneurons suppress these behaviors to promote long-range dispersal. Downstream motor neurons encode specific movement parameters: SMD sets omega turn amplitude, RIV specifies the ventral bias of post-reversal turns, and SMB sets sinusoidal movement amplitude. The same circuit components are implicated in chemotaxis and thermotaxis, suggesting a shared substrate for multiple navigation strategies.

worthy-2018-plos-one.label: Worthy et al., PLOS ONE 2018
worthy-2018-plos-one.synopsis: Characterizes volatile odorants produced by preferred bacteria that guide food choice in C. elegans.

zhang-2016-jbc.label: Zhang et al., J Biol Chem 2016
zhang-2016-jbc.synopsis: Describes a 'Trojan Horse' mechanism by which harmful bacteria produce attractive odorants that lure C. elegans, causing olfactory deception that leads to ingestion of a harmful food source.

schiffer-2021-plos-pathogens.label: Schiffer et al., PLOS Pathogens 2021
schiffer-2021-plos-pathogens.synopsis: Demonstrates that C. elegans uses hydrogen peroxide — a bacterially-produced chemical — as a sensory signal to identify environmental niches offering both food and protection from oxidative stress. Shows that chemosensory evaluation extends beyond food location to include environmental safety assessment.

avery-1989-neuron.label: Avery & Horvitz, Neuron 1989
avery-1989-neuron.synopsis: Uses laser ablation to show that pharyngeal feeding requires two separately controlled muscle motions: isthmus peristalsis, driven solely by the M4 neuron, and pumping, stimulated by MC neurons in response to food but capable of continuing without them. Destroying the entire pharyngeal nervous system fails to abolish pumping, suggesting an autonomous myogenic rhythm. Establishes the basic circuit architecture of feeding-rate control and notes that most of the C. elegans nervous system is dispensable for viability under laboratory conditions.

avery-2003-j-exp-biol.label: Avery & Shtonda, J Exp Biol 2003
avery-2003-j-exp-biol.synopsis: Uses video analysis and hydrodynamic simulation to explain how the C. elegans pharynx transports bacteria posteriorly despite operating at low Reynolds number, where purely reciprocal motions produce no net transport. Delayed relaxation of the isthmus relative to the corpus, combined with particle acceleration at the center of the pharyngeal lumen, generates efficient net posterior particle movement. The M3 inhibitory neuron controls relaxation timing and is critical for transport; the model predicts and confirms that smaller bacteria are more efficiently transported and thus better food sources.

maguire-2011-curr-biol.label: Maguire et al., Curr Biol 2011
maguire-2011-curr-biol.synopsis: Shows that C. elegans uses anterior touch mechanosensory neurons to detect constricting hyphal rings of predacious Drechslerella fungi and escape via reversal. Escape requires not only reversal but tyramine-dependent suppression of exploratory head movements: tyramine released by RIM neurons acts via the LGC-55 channel in neck muscles and AVB neurons to coordinate backward locomotion with head immobilization, enabling smooth retraction from the ring. Tyramine signaling mutants (tdc-1, lgc-55) reverse normally but fail to suppress head movements and are caught more often in competition assays, demonstrating that this motor coordination has genuine selective value and likely reflects an evolutionary arms race between nematodes and nematophagous fungi.

hsueh-2017-elife.label: Hsueh et al., eLife 2017
hsueh-2017-elife.synopsis: Shows that the nematophagous fungus Arthrobotrys oligospora attracts C. elegans by producing volatile olfactory mimics of food and sex cues. GC-MS analysis identified several attractive volatiles including sulfurous food-odor mimics and methyl 3-methyl-2-butenoate (MMB), a compound that elicits strong sex- and stage-specific attraction in adult hermaphrodites and females across Caenorhabditis species while interfering with mating — consistent with mimicry of a male sex pheromone. Attraction is mediated by AWC olfactory neurons. AWC-defective animals are caught less frequently, demonstrating a direct fitness cost of olfactory mimicry and suggesting an evolutionary arms race between nematodes and predacious fungi.

yu-2021-nat-commun.label: Yu et al., Nat Commun 2021
yu-2021-nat-commun.synopsis: Shows that the nematode-trapping fungus Duddingtonia flagrans uses 6-methyl-salicylic acid (6-MSA), a polyketide synthase product, as both a morphogen controlling spatiotemporal trap formation and a chemoattractant that lures C. elegans into fungal colonies. 6-MSA and its downstream metabolites arthrosporols both inhibit trap formation; the presence of nematodes suppresses 6-MSA and arthrosporol biosynthesis, enabling traps to form. Reveals 6-MSA as a quorum-sensing-like interkingdom signal mediating fungal predator-prey communication.

lin-2025-isci.label: Lin et al., iScience 2025
lin-2025-isci.synopsis: Shows that Arthrobotrys oligospora predation induces behavioral quiescence in C. elegans, dependent on activation of the sleep-promoting neurons ALA and RIS. Mechanosensation contributes to this quiescent state, suggesting that mechanical stress from fungal constriction activates the sleep/stress circuit. Provides insight into how prey nervous systems respond to active predation as a physiological stressor distinct from simple touch.

zaslaver-2015-pnas.label: Zaslaver et al., PNAS 2015
zaslaver-2015-pnas.synopsis: Examines sparse coding in the C. elegans olfactory system; characterizes how odor identity is represented and compressed across layers of the sensory circuit.

meisel-2014-cell.label: Meisel et al., Cell 2014
meisel-2014-cell.synopsis: Characterizes chemosensory detection of pathogen-produced secondary metabolites by C. elegans and the behavioral consequences.

moore-2019a-cell.label: Moore et al., Cell 2019
moore-2019a-cell.synopsis: Characterizes pathogen avoidance learning and its transgenerational transmission in C. elegans.

kaletsky-2020-nature.label: Kaletsky et al., Nature 2020
kaletsky-2020-nature.synopsis: Demonstrates transgenerational inheritance of pathogen-specific small RNAs that confer avoidance behavior in offspring.

moore-2021-cell.label: Moore et al., Cell 2021
moore-2021-cell.synopsis: Demonstrates that C. elegans co-opts Cer1 retrotransposon-encoded virus-like particles to transmit learned pathogen avoidance between animals and across generations. Cer1 mediates inter-tissue signaling from the germline to neurons required for inherited avoidance memory; wild strains carrying Cer1 can learn and inherit small-RNA-induced avoidance, revealing a genomic element co-opted for adaptive immune memory.

melo-2012-cell.label: Melo & Ruvkun, Cell 2012
melo-2012-cell.synopsis: Disruption of core cellular processes (translation, respiration, protein turnover) triggers avoidance of normally attractive bacteria via a neuroendocrine axis requiring serotonin and Jnk signaling, suggesting C. elegans detects pathogens indirectly through surveillance of host cellular integrity.

prakash-2021-embo-j.label: Prakash et al., EMBO J 2021
prakash-2021-embo-j.synopsis: Identifies 1-undecene from Pseudomonas aeruginosa as a volatile pathogen signal detected by C. elegans olfactory neurons, triggering a flight-or-fight behavioral response and demonstrating that bacterial volatiles can function as microbe-associated molecular patterns.

sternson-2013-curr-opin-neurobiol.label: Sternson et al., Curr Opin Neurobiol 2013
sternson-2013-curr-opin-neurobiol.synopsis: Review of neural circuits for hunger motivation across animals; contextualizes C. elegans feeding circuits within broader principles of hunger-driven behavior.

rengarajan-2019-pnas.label: Rengarajan et al., PNAS 2019
rengarajan-2019-pnas.synopsis: Feeding state reconfigures sensory valence in C. elegans — the same odor can drive attraction or aversion depending on hunger state, demonstrating that motivational state rewires sensory circuit outputs.

jang-2019-pnas.label: Jang et al., PNAS 2019
jang-2019-pnas.synopsis: Shows that C. elegans learns to avoid salt concentrations associated with starvation, requiring integrated input from two taste neurons — ASER (the primary salt sensor) and ASG (newly implicated) — to bias turning behavior and navigate toward food after food deprivation.

ryu-2018-embo-j.label: Ryu et al., EMBO J 2018
ryu-2018-embo-j.synopsis: Pheromone-mediated avoidance is regulated by insulin signaling, connecting metabolic state to chemosensory valence and revealing how internal nutritional state modulates social chemical signaling.

matty-2022-plos-genetics.label: Matty et al., PLOS Genetics 2022
matty-2022-plos-genetics.synopsis: Intestine-to-neuronal intertissue signaling during food deprivation alters risk-taking behavior in C. elegans; gut-derived signals shift the explore/exploit balance toward riskier food-seeking strategies.

chao-2004-nat-neurosci.label: Chao et al., Nat Neurosci 2004
chao-2004-nat-neurosci.synopsis: Serotonin modulates the threshold of ASH-mediated nociceptive avoidance in C. elegans, showing how neuromodulator tone adjusts the sensitivity of aversive sensory responses based on internal state.

hughes-2021-g3.label: Hughes et al., G3 2021
hughes-2021-g3.synopsis: C. elegans has a single PIEZO mechanosensory channel ortholog (pezo-1) with multiple predicted isoforms expressed in distinct tissues. Longer isoforms in pharyngeal muscles and glands are required for normal food-evoked responses, while shorter isoforms are expressed in neurons. Establishes C. elegans as a model for studying functional divergence among PIEZO channel family members in the context of feeding.

bayer-2025-curr-biol.label: Bayer et al., Curr Biol 2025
bayer-2025-curr-biol.synopsis: Identifies DEGT-1, a DEG/ENaC ion channel in four pharyngeal neurons, as a proprioceptor that detects shear forces generated by the pharynx's own pumping movement. Worms lacking DEGT-1 feed abnormally fast; restoring it in just two neurons rescues this phenotype. Shows that the feeding organ monitors its own mechanical activity to regulate pump rate — an internal feedback loop rather than external food sensing.

filipowicz-2021-elife.label: Filipowicz et al., eLife 2021
filipowicz-2021-elife.synopsis: Two TRPM channels (GON-2 and GTL-2) mediate rapid avoidance of the pathogen Enterococcus faecalis by detecting intestinal distension as bacteria colonize the gut. Multiple sensory neuron classes (ASE, AWB, AWC) and the NPR-1 oxygen-sensing pathway converge to produce this response. Demonstrates that gut distension — a physical consequence of colonization — is itself a sensory signal that triggers protective behavior.

park-2024-nat-commun.label: Park et al., Nat Commun 2024
park-2024-nat-commun.synopsis: The PIEZO mechanosensory channel (pezo-1), expressed in the non-neuronal pharyngeal-intestinal valve, detects food accumulation in the intestinal lumen and triggers rhythmic pharyngeal contractions for swallowing. Mammalian PIEZO1 can substitute for pezo-1 in this context. Optogenetic stimulation of the valve reproduces swallowing behavior, revealing how interoceptive gut signals coordinate the mechanics of food intake.

rhoades-2019-cell.label: Rhoades et al., Cell 2019
rhoades-2019-cell.synopsis: Acid-sensing ion channels DEL-7 and DEL-3 in the NSM enteric serotonergic neuron allow it to sense food ingestion directly and slow locomotion during feeding. NSM acts as an interoceptive detector of what is being consumed, not just whether food is present nearby. Defines a molecular mechanism by which the enteric nervous system translates the act of eating into a sustained change in foraging behavior.

estrem-2026-curr-biol.label: Estrem et al., Curr Biol 2026
estrem-2026-curr-biol.synopsis: Polysaccharides and peptidoglycans from beneficial bacteria activate the enteric neuron NSM through DEL-3/DEL-7 acid-sensing ion channels, reducing locomotion and promoting feeding. The pathogen Serratia marcescens produces prodigiosin, a molecule that specifically blocks NSM activation by these bacterial signals — a mechanism by which pathogens disrupt the worm's ability to recognize and respond to its normal microbiota.

feng-2025-nat-commun.label: Feng et al., Nat Commun 2025
feng-2025-nat-commun.synopsis: Identifies 22 E. coli metabolic mutants that induce aversion and stress responses in C. elegans, using genome-wide bacterial screening to probe how diet quality shapes foraging behavior. Different classes of serotonergic neurons promote aversion to non-preferred diets or retention on preferred diets through distinct serotonin receptors, revealing that a single neuromodulator drives opposing behavioral outcomes depending on circuit context. Serotonin is integrated with dopamine and octopamine across distributed circuits to generate context-dependent evaluation of dietary quality.

hyun-2016-sci-rep.label: Hyun et al., Sci Rep 2016
hyun-2016-sci-rep.synopsis: Mutations in the SREBP-SCD fat biosynthesis pathway reduce satiety quiescence in C. elegans. RNAi screening identifies an acetyl-CoA carboxylase as critical for normal satiety responses, and 11 nuclear receptors individually influence both fat storage and feeding behavior. Links major lipid metabolic pathways to behavioral regulation of food intake.

flavell-2013-cell.label: Flavell et al., Cell 2013
flavell-2013-cell.synopsis: Serotonin and the neuropeptide PDF (pigment-dispersing factor) drive opposing sustained behavioral states in C. elegans: serotonin acting via the MOD-1 channel promotes dwelling (slow, local foraging), while PDF acting via a Gs-coupled receptor promotes roaming (fast, exploratory movement). These neuromodulators produce behavioral states with distinct temporal dynamics that outlast the triggering stimulus, revealing how global modulatory signals generate persistent changes in behavioral mode.

you-2008-cell-metab.label: You et al., Cell Metab 2008
you-2008-cell-metab.synopsis: C. elegans enters a quiescent state — cessation of eating and movement — after consuming nutrient-rich food, intensified by prior fasting. This satiety response is regulated by insulin, TGF-beta, and cGMP signaling, with the EGL-4 cGMP-dependent kinase acting in ASI sensory neurons downstream of both pathways. Proposes C. elegans as a model for conserved appetite-suppression mechanisms, with functional parallels to mammalian satiety signaling.

benarous-2009-plos-one.label: Ben Arous et al., PLoS ONE 2009
benarous-2009-plos-one.synopsis: C. elegans alternates between dwelling and roaming behavioral states in a food-concentration-dependent manner. External sensory input through amphid neurons extends roaming, while internal nutritional sensing of food quality promotes dwelling. Serotonin, insulin, and TGF-beta pathways act on different timescales: biogenic amines enable rapid environmental adaptation, while peptide signals mediate slower integration of nutritional history.

choi-2013-neuron.label: Choi et al., Neuron 2013
choi-2013-neuron.synopsis: NPR-1 and its neuropeptide ligands FLP-18 and FLP-21 are required for locomotion quiescence during larval lethargus. The arousal neuropeptide PDF-1 from central neurons opposes quiescence; when PDF-1 secretion decreases, quiescence ensues. PDF receptors on peripheral mechanosensory neurons amplify touch sensitivity during arousal, revealing how a central neuromodulatory state gates peripheral sensory processing.

sze-2000-nature.label: Sze et al., Nature 2000
sze-2000-nature.synopsis: The single C. elegans tryptophan hydroxylase gene tph-1 is required for all serotonin biosynthesis. Mutants lacking serotonin eat less, lay fewer eggs, store excess fat, and some enter the dauer diapause state. TGF-beta and insulin-like neuroendocrine signals are partially disrupted in these animals. The metabolic and feeding phenotypes parallel effects of serotonergic dysregulation on appetite and obesity in mammals.

davis-2018-sci-rep.label: Davis et al., Sci Rep 2018
davis-2018-sci-rep.synopsis: ASI and ASH sensory neurons act antagonistically to regulate satiety decisions: starvation decreases ASH responsiveness while enhancing ASI activity, and ablating either neuron produces opposite behavioral effects on feeding. This push-pull circuit resolves competing sensory signals — appetitive vs aversive — to generate context-appropriate eating decisions based on internal nutritional state.

gallagher-2013-j-neurosci.label: Gallagher et al., J Neurosci 2013
gallagher-2013-j-neurosci.synopsis: The ASI amphid neuron pair controls feeding-state transitions through TGF-beta signaling: ASI-derived TGF-beta ligands act on downstream RIM and RIC neurons to suppress dwelling and promote quiescence after sufficient food intake. Mutations in the TGF-beta receptor or downstream SMADs increase food consumption and reduce satiety behavior. cGMP signaling in ASI contributes alongside TGF-beta, placing ASI as a central integrator of nutritional state and sleep-like behavioral transitions.

millet-2025-elife.label: Millet et al., eLife 2025
millet-2025-elife.synopsis: C. elegans devalues food sources that are harder to access in a manner consistent with effort discounting models from behavioral economics. Worms show differential patch-leaving rates based on the cost of accessing food, and this cost-benefit weighting depends on dopamine signaling. Establishes C. elegans as an invertebrate model for studying the neural basis of effort-based decision-making in foraging.

bonnard-2022-elife.label: Bonnard et al., eLife 2022
bonnard-2022-elife.synopsis: PharaGlow is an open-source imaging and analysis pipeline that simultaneously measures pharyngeal pumping and locomotion in up to 50 unrestrained C. elegans. Built on standard fluorescence microscopy and a Python workflow, it captures feeding dynamics across developmental stages, genetic perturbations, and food conditions at single-worm resolution. Provides a high-throughput tool for quantifying feeding behavior as an integrated readout of nutritional state.

worthy-2018-chem-senses.label: Worthy et al., Chem Senses 2018
worthy-2018-chem-senses.synopsis: Identifies the volatile blend that C. elegans uses to recognize the pathogen Serratia marcescens. Of five major volatiles released by the bacterium, only acetone and 2-butanone drive attraction, both detected by AWC^ON neurons. Reveals the molecular specificity underlying olfactory pathogen recognition — the worm is attracted to, not repelled by, these specific signals.

choi-2015-isme-j.label: Choi et al., ISME J 2015
choi-2015-isme-j.synopsis: C. elegans is attracted to lactic acid bacteria through olfactory detection of diacetyl, a fermentation byproduct produced in the presence of citrate. Wild nematodes isolated from decomposing fruit show attraction to diacetyl from co-isolated bacteria, demonstrating an ecologically relevant chemosensory interaction. Grounds the well-characterized diacetyl/AWA olfactory response in a natural host-microbiome context.

choi-2022-curr-biol.label: Choi et al., Curr Biol 2022
choi-2022-curr-biol.synopsis: A single chemosensory GPCR, SRI-14, expressed in two distinct neuron types mediates opposite behavioral responses to dimethyl trisulfide depending on concentration: attraction at low levels, avoidance at high. The same receptor in different circuit contexts generates opposing outputs, showing how concentration-dependent valence switching can emerge from a shared molecular detector without requiring separate receptors for attraction and repulsion.

prakash-2022-biorxiv.label: Prakash et al., bioRxiv 2022
prakash-2022-biorxiv.synopsis: Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces pyrrole, a volatile heterocyclic compound that attracts C. elegans via AWA sensory neurons. In the presence of competing odor cues, pyrrole influences food choice toward P. aeruginosa despite its pathogenicity. Illustrates how a single bacterial volatile can shape olfactory decision-making in a multi-odor environment.

siddiqui-2026-elife.label: Siddiqui et al., eLife 2026
siddiqui-2026-elife.synopsis: Shows that C. elegans uses olfaction to select leucine-supplemented bacteria from its native microbiota. Leucine-supplemented bacteria produce isoamyl alcohol (IAA) in highest abundance; prior adaptation to IAA diminishes the diet preference, indicating habituation. Preference requires AWC olfactory neurons, and SNIF-1 (formerly SRD-12), a GPCR in AWC, is identified as a receptor for IAA and mediator of dietary decisions. Defines a receptor-ligand module linking olfactory detection of a bacterial metabolite to foraging for essential amino acid-rich diets.

pradel-2007-pnas.label: Pradel et al., PNAS 2007
pradel-2007-pnas.synopsis: C. elegans detects serrawettin W2, a cyclic lipodepsipentapeptide secreted by pathogenic Serratia marcescens, and avoids bacterial lawns producing it. Avoidance requires AWB chemosensory neurons and the toll-like receptor tol-1. Identifies a molecular pathogen-associated pattern recognized by the gustatory system, showing how taste contributes to innate immune-like food rejection.

brissette-2024-sci-adv.label: Brissette et al., Sci Adv 2024
brissette-2024-sci-adv.synopsis: Polyamines — cadaverine, putrescine, and spermidine — produced by E. coli activate chemosensory neurons and AIB interneurons to drive positive chemotaxis toward nutritive bacteria. The same circuit detects signals from the pathogen Enterococcus faecalis through different sensory inputs. Identifies polyamines as a class of microbe-derived chemical identifiers that help C. elegans distinguish beneficial from harmful bacteria.

kauffman-2010-plos-biol.label: Kauffman et al., PLoS Biol 2010
kauffman-2010-plos-biol.synopsis: Establishes a system for studying associative learning, short-term memory, and long-term associative memory in C. elegans through chemotaxis assays, demonstrating that worms form positive associations between a neutral chemoattractant and food. Long-term but not short-term associative memory requires crh-1, the C. elegans CREB homolog, whose expression declines with age and correlates with memory performance. Insulin/IGF-1 signaling (daf-2 mutants) improves early adult memory and maintains learning ability with age; dietary restriction (eat-2 mutants) impairs long-term memory in young adults but maintains it longer. Reveals that longevity pathways have distinct and sometimes opposing effects on cognitive aging through their regulation of crh-1.

chalasani-2010-nat-neurosci.label: Chalasani et al., Nat Neurosci 2010
chalasani-2010-nat-neurosci.synopsis: Shows that neuropeptide signals released by interneurons feed back onto AWC olfactory neurons, modifying the dynamics of their odor-evoked calcium responses. Demonstrates that circuit feedback can tune primary sensory representations, with implications for adaptation and gain control in chemosensory processing.

shtonda-2006-j-exp-biol.label: Shtonda & Avery, J Exp Biol 2006
shtonda-2006-j-exp-biol.synopsis: Demonstrates that C. elegans exhibits active dietary choice: worms leave low-quality or hard-to-eat bacteria and hunt for nutritionally superior food sources, a preference enhanced by prior experience with good food. During food seeking, worms alternate between dwelling (frequent stops and reversals) and roaming (rapid straight movement); roaming is suppressed on good food and extended on bad food. AIY interneurons are required to extend roaming periods and are essential for efficient dietary search, linking interneuron activity to the explore/exploit balance during foraging.
